nodes.title: What kind of image is it?
nodes.description: Answer a few short questions about your image. You get advice straight away on whether it needs alt text and what to write.

options.label: Decorative
options.description: Mood shots, backgrounds, icons next to text

options.label: Informative
options.description: Charts, diagrams, photos carrying information that matters

options.label: Clickable or functional
options.description: Buttons, links, icons that carry out an action

options.label: Logo
options.description: The logo of an organisation or a brand

options.label: Image of text
options.description: A screenshot, a poster, or any other text as an image

nodes.title: If you leave the image out, is any information lost?
nodes.description: Think about whether the image adds something that is not already in the text.

options.label: Yes, information is lost
options.description: The image holds information that appears nowhere else

options.label: No, the image is purely decorative
options.description: The information is already in the text, or it is a mood shot

nodes.title: Decorative image
nodes.advice: The image is decorative. Hide it from assistive technology.
solutions: On an <svg>: leave out the <title> and <desc> elements, or add aria-hidden="true"
examples: Icons next to text that says the same thing
Images whose information is already written out in text

nodes.title: What kind of informative image is this?
nodes.description: Work out whether the image stands on its own, is clickable, or turns out to be decorative after all.

options.label: Informative
options.description: Holds information that is not written out on the page and is needed to understand the content

options.label: Clickable without text
options.description: The image is a link or a button, with no text beside it

options.label: Clickable with text
options.description: The image is a link or a button, with text beside it

options.label: Decorative after all
options.description: The image adds no information of its own

nodes.title: How much information does the image hold?
nodes.description: Work out whether a short description is enough, or whether you need a longer explanation.

options.label: Short and simple
options.description: You can describe the image in two or three lines

options.label: Complex, a lot of data
options.description: The image holds a lot of information, such as a detailed chart or diagram

nodes.title: Short description
nodes.advice: Write short, clear alt text that carries the information that matters.
solutions: Or put a sentence or a table directly above or below the image
examples: alt="Bar chart of visitor growth in 2024. Monthly average 300, highest 400 in May."

nodes.title: Complex image
nodes.advice: A complex image needs two text alternatives.
solutions: 1. Short alt text that points to the longer description. For example: alt="Visitor numbers in 2024, chart. Full description below the image"
2. A longer explanation below the image: a full description in text, a table with the data, or a file to download

nodes.title: Does the clickable image have text with it?
nodes.description: A functional image carries out an action, as a button or a link.

options.label: Image only, no text
options.description: For example a magnifying glass icon used as a search button

options.label: Image and text
options.description: For example an icon with the word "Search" next to it

nodes.title: Clickable image without text
nodes.advice: The alt text describes what the image does, not what it looks like.
solutions: You can use aria-label="..." instead if you know what you are doing

nodes.title: Does the visible text already explain enough?
nodes.description: Check whether the text next to the image already makes the action clear.

options.label: Yes, the text is enough
options.description: The image adds nothing to what the action is

options.label: No, context is missing
options.description: The image adds context that is not in the text

nodes.title: The image is redundant
nodes.advice: The visible text already makes the action clear, so assistive technology does not need the image.
solutions: Use alt="" so screen readers skip the image

nodes.title: The image adds context
nodes.advice: Write alt text that describes the context the image adds.
solutions: Describe what the image adds to the action. For example: alt="PDF"

nodes.title: Is the logo clickable?
nodes.description: A logo that links somewhere, usually the homepage, needs different alt text from a logo that just sits on the page.

options.label: No, the logo is not clickable
options.description: The logo sits on the page as an image, without a link

options.label: Yes, the logo is a link
options.description: The logo links to another page, usually the homepage

nodes.title: Static logo
nodes.advice: Use the name of the organisation as the alt text.

nodes.title: Clickable logo
nodes.advice: The alt text has to carry the text in the logo and make the destination clear.
solutions: For example: alt="City of Amsterdam, to the homepage"

nodes.title: Could you put the text on the page as real text instead?
nodes.description: Text inside an image is hard to read, does not scale and is not accessible.

options.label: Yes, real text is possible
options.description: The text can go on the page as HTML

options.label: No, it is art or design
options.description: For example a poster, calligraphy or an artistic design

nodes.title: Use real text
nodes.advice: Put the text on the page as real HTML instead of an image. Text inside an image is hard to read and not accessible.
solutions: Replace the image with real text, styled with CSS
Use a web font if the typeface matters

nodes.title: Describe the text in the alt text
nodes.advice: Describe the text that appears in the image.
solutions: For example: alt="Poster reading 'Freedom for everyone' in handwritten lettering"

tips: Do not repeat text that is already visible
Ask yourself: what does someone need to know if they cannot see this?
